completion.text: {"voice_profile":"Third-person autobiography in which the elderly Adams treats his younger and present self with ironic detachment ('Adams', 'one', 'the student', 'the tourist', 'an insect', 'the monkey'). Long periodic sentences turn on qualification and paradox. Cosmic science metaphors (force, mass, inertia, triangulation, attraction) are applied to politics and friendship. He undercuts himself constantly through self-deprecation and mock-pedantry. He flatly refuses certainty ('knew no more than...'). Aphoristic closers end paragraphs. Foreign tags and verse quotations act as punctuation. Grief appears only obliquely, through restraint and stage-images. Double hyphens mark interruption and accumulation.","book_context":"Late in the book, after an omitted chapter of travel and silence, Adams reaches sixty while his closest friends hold power. John Hay is ambassador in London and then Secretary of State; Lodge is a Senator; Roosevelt follows. Clarence King and Hay are declining. The recurring mechanisms carry forward: 'a friend in power is a friend lost'; sitting on the steps of Ara Coeli; Pteraspis, Lyell and Limulus from the Darwinism chapter; women and the Virgin as force; and the search for unity against multiplicity, now recast as attempts to measure history mechanically. These chapters move from diplomatic triumph to the dynamo and the Virgin, then to magnets, geology and Russian inertia. They prepare the formal 'Dynamic Theory' and the 'Law of Acceleration'.
